article_content: NASA and Japan are teaming up to launch the world's first satellite made of wood, named LignoSat, with a target launch year of 2024. This innovative mission is designed to help solve the problem of space debris by using materials that completely burn up upon re-entry, ensuring no harmful remnants are left in space or fall back to Earth. LignoSat is being developed in partnership by NASA, the Japanese space agency JAXA, and Kyoto University, spearheaded by Kyoto University researcher Koji Murata. The team has experimented with various types of wood—magnolia, cherry, and birch—testing their performance in space, including sending samples to the International Space Station to see how they withstand space conditions. The final design uses magnolia for the satellite's structure, chosen for its consistent and strong cellular makeup. Measuring 10 centimeters on each side and weighing about one kilogram, LignoSat features a camera and sensors for data collection regarding its status in orbit, and is coated to shield it from ultraviolet and cosmic rays. The wooden satellite will be launched as an additional payload alongside other satellites. Specific launch site and timing are still being decided, but the launch is targeted for 2024. LignoSat will orbit Earth at about 500 kilometers for several months before safely burning up during atmospheric re-entry. The project’s main objective is to evaluate wood’s potential as a material for future space missions, paving the way for more sustainable spacecraft components and possibly influencing designs for habitats or equipment on the Moon, Mars, and other space destinations.

LignoSat tas fram i samarbete mellan NASA, den japanska rymdmyndigheten JAXA och Kyoto University, under ledning av forskaren Koji Murata på Kyoto University. Teamet har testat olika träslag—magnolia, körsbär och björk—och undersökt hur de klarar rymdens påfrestningar, bland annat med försök på internationella rymdstationen. Den slutliga konstruktionen använder magnoliaträ för satellitens stomme, då det har en jämn och hållbar cellstruktur. LignoSat är en kub som mäter 10 centimeter per sida och väger cirka ett kilogram. Den är utrustad med en kamera och sensorer som rapporterar om dess tillstånd i omloppsbana, samt har en beläggning som skyddar mot ultravioletta och kosmiska strålar. Satelliten kommer att skjutas upp som extra last tillsammans med andra satelliter. Exakt uppskjutningsplats och datum är inte bestämt, men målet är uppskjutning 2024. LignoSat kommer att gå i omloppsbana omkring 500 kilometer över jorden i flera månader innan den säkert förintas vid inträde i atmosfären. Syftet är att undersöka om trä kan vara ett hållbart material för framtida rymdfärder, vilket kan öppna upp för miljövänliga lösningar och påverka design av utrustning och boplatser på månen, Mars och andra destinationer i rymden.

article_content: Rachel Sawford, 29, from Portsmouth, overcame an abusive relationship to earn a 2:1 degree in Social Work from the University of Portsmouth. When she visited the Jobcentre seeking employment advice, she was told by staff to remove her degree from her CV, as it could 'scare off' employers who might see her as overqualified for available positions. Rachel expressed disappointment at this advice, feeling it undermined years of effort and rendered her degree worthless. Despite her desire to find work and leave benefits, she refuses to omit her achievement from her CV. A mother-of-one who graduated in July, Rachel had aimed to use her degree to help vulnerable women but has struggled to find related employment. She is currently on a four-week placement as a substitute teaching assistant but has yet to secure future employment. Jobcentre staff advised that she would be 'more employable' for certain roles if she left out her degree, particularly for positions not requiring such qualifications. Rachel disagreed with this recommendation, insisting that her qualification reflects her hard work and skills. She remains determined to find work in social work, support, or youth projects. According to recent Office for National Statistics data, about half of recent graduates are in jobs that do not require a degree. The Department for Work and Pensions indicated that Jobcentre advisors assist jobseekers in tailoring their CVs to best match relevant roles. Nearly 40% of people over the age of 21 are now graduates, compared to 17% in 1992. The University of Portsmouth reports that 93% of its social work graduates are employed six months post-graduation, although the proportion in graduate-level positions is unclear.

article_content: Thomas Bagley, a Duke University student and Phi Delta Theta fraternity pledge majoring in computer science and mathematics, recently revealed the identity of his classmate, Belle Knox, as an adult film actress financing her tuition through her work in the industry. After recognizing her from online videos, Bagley publicized Knox’s identity, leading to significant backlash against him both for his actions and his own consumption of adult content. Mike Kulich, president of Monarchy Distribution, a pornography distribution company, publicly criticized Bagley for exposing Knox while himself being a consumer of the industry. Kulich estimated Bagley’s spending at $200 per week on adult sites and sarcastically thanked him for his support. Belle Knox turned to the adult film industry to pay Duke’s $47,000 annual tuition. She has since appeared in cable news interviews and contributed op-eds discussing her experiences and the relationship between pornography and feminism. She reports mixed responses from students, with support coming primarily from the LGBTQ community and hostility from some 'frat guys' and certain female peers. Both Bagley and Knox have experienced online harassment; Bagley deactivated his Twitter account amid the controversy and expressed regret in an interview, saying, 'I certainly would take it back.' Knox reported feeling unsafe following her exposure and was allowed a brief break from classes. Knox explained in interviews that she initially concealed her involvement in adult films from her family, a decision she now regrets, but insists it hasn’t affected their relationship. She has stated she would support her own daughter in making an informed career choice, including in sex work. Knox’s stage name draws inspiration from the character Belle in 'Beauty and the Beast,' the British drama 'Secret Diary of a Call Girl,' and the surname Knox, referencing Amanda Knox. Despite the challenges and harassment, she remains steadfast in her decisions.
